meta.title: Penalties Sized to the Gain: PhD catch-up
meta.author: Ameer Alhashemi

slides.title: Penalties Sized to the Gain
slides.subtitle: When do random audits stop AI agents from over-using a shared resource?
slides.notes: One sentence: I study when spot-checks stop AI agents from taking more than their share of something they share, and whether the penalty that does it can be worked out in advance.

slides.title: The Project in One Slide

cards.label: Why
cards.head: Oversight of AI agents is sampled
cards.text: AI agents are starting to act on resources they share with others, such as compute, energy and budgets. Whoever oversees them can usually check only a few of their actions.

cards.label: What I built
cards.head: A shared resource with checks
cards.text: Six agents draw on one renewable resource over many rounds. A reviewer sets how much each may take, and a few agents are checked at random each round.

cards.label: What I tested
cards.head: Consequences and penalty size
cards.text: What a caught agent should face (a fine, a memory of the offence, or both), and whether the fine that stops an agent can be predicted before it is tried.

cards.label: What I found
cards.head: Checks work through consequences
cards.text: Checks reduced harm only when a catch had a consequence. The stopping fine could be predicted from how much an agent gains by over-taking, for programmed agents and for language models.

slides.notes: If people remember one slide, it should be this one. The rest of the talk unpacks each card.
slides.takeaway: The rest of the talk: the setting, three questions, how I test them, five findings, and what is still running

slides.title: The Problem

blocks.head: A limited, shared resource
blocks.text: Each agent receives an allowance: the amount it may take this round. Taking more helps that agent and leaves less for everyone else.

blocks.head: Oversight by sampling
blocks.text: Checking every action costs too much, so an overseer spot-checks a few, as tax and fisheries inspectors do.

blocks.head: The open question
blocks.text: When does a sampled check stop agents taking more than their allowance, and how large does the penalty need to be?

slides.caption: The same question in three settings, chosen because one agent's over-use reaches others in a different way in each: through a single shared pool (Fishery), through damage to direct neighbours (Forest), and through harm that appears only when two kinds of use combine (River). A result that holds in all three does not rest on one structure.
slides.notes: These settings are not toys to be solved one by one; they are a way of checking that a result about oversight holds across the main ways harm can spread.

items.head: What has to follow a catch?
items.text: When a check finds an agent taking more than its allowance, the overseer can fine it, remember it, or do nothing. Which of these reduces harm?

items.head: Can the stopping fine be predicted?
items.text: Is there a fine size at which over-taking stops, and can it be worked out before that fine is tried?

items.head: Do language models behave the same way?
items.text: When most agents are language models making their own choices, do they stop where the prediction says?

slides.title: How One Round Works
slides.caption: Each round, every agent asks for a share; the reviewer predicts what the requests would do to the resource and scales them all by one factor; each agent then takes its allowance or more; the resource regrows; and a few agents are checked at random.
slides.takeaway: Harm = the resource falling below half its capacity, the level at which it regrows fastest
slides.notes: Half capacity is the maximum-sustainable-yield level used in fisheries management. The same harm line is used in all three settings.

slides.title: How I Test It

steps.head: Run the setting
steps.text: Six agents share the resource for many rounds; the reviewer sets allowances; a few agents are checked at random each round.

steps.head: Measure the gain
steps.text: Run games without any fine and record how much an agent gains from one round of taking more than its allowance.

steps.head: Predict, then freeze
steps.text: Work out the fine that should stop over-taking and record the prediction before any game with that fine is run.

steps.head: Test on games the prediction never saw
steps.text: Run the predicted fine and the fines around it on new games, and report the result whether or not it matches.

quantities.meaning: chance that an agent is checked in a round (1 in 6 for the language models)
fine paid when a check finds an agent over its allowance
expected fine for one round of over-taking
what an agent gains from one round of over-taking
the prediction: over-taking stops once the expected fine is larger than the gain (Becker 1968)

slides.notes: Example: with a 1 in 6 chance of a check and a 30 t fine, the expected fine is 5 t; a model that gains about 4.5 t per round should stop there, and should not stop at 24 t (4 t expected).

slides.title: Finding 1: A Catch Needs a Consequence

blocks.head: The setting
blocks.text: Some agents report less than they intend to take, so the reviewer underestimates their use unless a check catches them.

blocks.head: Checks without memory
blocks.text: Correcting only the round in which a lie was caught removed 10–46% of the harm.

blocks.head: Checks with memory
blocks.text: Remembering each caught lie and adjusting that agent's later allowances reduced harm in all 12 settings tested. In Fishery, rounds below half capacity fell from 43–99% to 0.3–3%.

slides.caption: Share of rounds below half capacity when some agents under-report. Dark: no checks. Light: checks without memory. Green: checks with memory. Each group has four settings: 2 or 4 misbehaving agents (2g, 4g) and two regrowth rates (1.0 and 0.85 of normal).
slides.notes: Programmed agents, 64 independent games per setting, 80 rounds each.

slides.title: Finding 2: A Predictable Threshold

blocks.head: What was predicted
blocks.text: Programmed agents choose how much to over-take so as to earn the most. From games without checks, we predicted the expected fine at which they would stop.

blocks.head: The result
blocks.text: In 5 of 5 new settings, the observed stopping point was within one step of the prediction.

blocks.head: Why this comes first
blocks.text: These agents are built to maximise their payoff, so this checks the measurement method before it is used on language models.

slides.caption: Observed against predicted stopping point (expected fine). Filled: new settings predicted in advance. Open: the checking rate, or the chance that a check catches the cheat, was varied. The band marks one step of the tested grid.
slides.notes: This is a validation, not a surprise: the agents optimise the payoff the prediction is based on.

slides.title: Finding 3: Two Shortcuts That Backfire

images.caption: Lowering every agent's allowance to make up for known cheaters let the cheaters gain more than with no checks at all (142 vs 113); honest agents paid for it.
Always checking the agent with the largest report caught 25% of liars over a game, against 100% with random checks: the largest reporter is often honest.

slides.takeaway: Shortcuts that save checks can open blind spots
slides.notes: Checking where the outcome fell furthest below the reviewer's forecast did best in Forest, so targeting by outcome can work; targeting by report did not.

slides.title: Finding 4: Language Models Stop Where Predicted
slides.caption: Four open language models each controlled four of the six fishers (520 games). Left: share of rounds in which a model took more than its allowance, at each fine, with a 1 in 6 chance of a check. Triangles: stopping fine predicted before testing (open) and observed (filled). Right: catch left for the two rule-following fishers.
slides.takeaway: Predicted before testing: 30 t. Observed: 30 t (Nemotron 3 Super), 24 t (gpt-oss-120b)
slides.notes: Gemma rarely took more than its allowance and Mistral never did, so they say nothing about the stopping fine. A small fine made gpt-oss over-take more (55% to about 90%), as if the fine were a price.

slides.title: Finding 5: One Round's Gain Matters

blocks.head: What predicted it
blocks.text: How much each model took above its allowance in one round without a fine (4.5–4.7 t).

blocks.head: What did not
blocks.text: What over-taking earned over a whole game: about −1 to +0.7 t per round, because over-taking depleted the lake.

blocks.head: Compared with an ideal optimiser
blocks.text: An agent that maximised its expected payoff would keep over-taking until 36 t. Both models stopped earlier, and gradually.

slides.caption: Each point compares a predicted and an observed stopping fine; points on the dashed line were predicted exactly.
slides.notes: This shows what predicts where the models stop, not why they stop.

slides.title: Memory Works for Language Models Too
slides.cardNote: gpt-oss-120b, no fine in either condition, 10 games each

blocks.head: Reduced, not stopped
blocks.text: Memory protected the lake without any fine, but some over-taking remained. For Nemotron 3 Super, over-taking fell from 65% to 33%.

blocks.head: With a large enough fine
blocks.text: Fines above the gain stopped over-taking and kept the harvest at 0.99 of the maximum the lake can sustain.

slides.title: Running Now (Results Soon)

rows.question: Expected fine, or the size of the fine?
rows.design: Same expected fine (2 t or 3 t), made up differently: 1 in 3 checked with a small fine, 1 in 6, or 1 in 12 with a large fine. gpt-oss-120b, 20 new games per condition.

rows.question: Does the prediction hold on new games?
rows.design: Stopping fine recorded in advance (30 t for both models), tested on 10 new games and with the rules reworded.

rows.question: What if nothing is ever checked?
rows.design: Rules that never mention checks, compared with checks that carry no fine.

rows.question: Does over-taking spread to neighbours?
rows.design: Forest: one programmed over-taker among five language-model agents; neighbours' cuts either hidden or visible.

slides.notes: A fifth model family, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, took more than its allowance in 80% of rounds without a fine; its predicted stopping fine (36 t) is recorded but not tested yet.

slides.title: Questions for You
questions: Is "taking more than your allowance" a fair stand-in for an AI agent misbehaving? What would be better?
If a fine works under one wording of the rules, how far would you trust it under another?
What would convince you more: more models, or more kinds of setting?
Where in your own work does someone check only a sample, and what happens after a catch?
